claims.text: The as-cast NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy has a relatively homogeneous, coarse-grained microstructure.
Heavy cold rolling at room temperature followed by annealing at 700–750 °C for a few minutes will trigger partial recrystallization in NbTaHfTiZrV0.5.
The proposed processing will create a heterogeneous microstructure containing both recrystallized grains and retained deformed regions.
The retained deformed regions will contain dislocation networks and subgrains.
Retained cold-worked regions will act as nucleation sites for deformation twins during subsequent mechanical loading.
Cold-worked regions reduce the critical resolved shear stress required to activate deformation twinning.
Activation of deformation twinning will increase strain hardening.
The increased strain hardening caused by deformation twinning will delay necking.
Recrystallized regions in the heterogeneous microstructure will preserve overall ductility.
The proposed processing will increase yield strength by approximately 10–20% relative to a fully recrystallized NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy.
The proposed processing will increase ultimate tensile strength by approximately 10–20% relative to a fully recrystallized NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy.
The proposed processing will maintain or improve plastic elongation relative to a fully recrystallized NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy.
Annealing for too long or at too high a temperature will cause full recrystallization and eliminate the retained twin-inducing cold-worked regions.
Insufficient annealing after heavy cold rolling may leave excessive work hardening and cause embrittlement.
The magnitude of the mechanical-property improvement may vary with processing variability.
Reproducibly obtaining the intended partially recrystallized microstructure requires precise process control.
